issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: The Maladaptive Strategies node mixes avoidance behaviours with what appears to be a trigger-like cue. 'Seeing people that I socialised with before the event' is phrased as a social reminder/trigger rather than a coping strategy, so within the specified node it is clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts' and 'Avoid Intimacy' imply social withdrawal, which can fit PTSD, but the specific target 'seeing people that I socialised with before the event' suggests avoidance of trauma reminders tied to the past. This sits awkwardly with the selected Negative Appraisals, which focus on incapacity, moral injury, and not belonging, without any corresponding interpersonal mistrust, shame in relationships, or reminder-based social threat theme.

issues.item: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: 'Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere' is possible in PTSD, but here it leans toward a broad identity/interpersonal alienation theme that is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The Threat items are predominantly hypervigilant safety-checking and pursuit fears, while the other appraisal items emphasize incapacity and violated values; this makes the belonging item feel disconnected rather than part of a coherent appraisal cluster.

vignette: Arjun Kumar, a 26-year-old South Asian man, had been a teller at a suburban branch of a major bank for the past four years when the day that would change his life arrived. It was a humid Thursday in October when a parked van outside the bank's lobby suddenly erupted in a spray of fire and smoke. The blast rattled the glass walls, and the metallic clatter of shattered glass echoed through the lobby. Arjun, in the middle of a routine cash-counting shift, was thrown to the floor, eyes wide as he watched the van's interior collapse into flames. He heard the screams of customers and the sirens of passing police cars. He survived, but the image of the car, the heat, the blood that slicked the concrete, and the helplessness of watching his coworkers flee left a scar that would stay with him for years. After the explosion, Arjun's nights became a series of restless awakenings. He would jolt awake, heart pounding, only to find himself sprawled on his bed, breathing hard as if the sound of an approaching vehicle was the only thing that could bring him back to safety. He would lie awake for hours, listening to the hum of traffic, glancing over his shoulder, and then turning around to make sure nothing was following him. Even in daylight, he would pause to scan the hallway of the bank, making sure no one was tailing him. The feeling of being in a constant state of vigilance was accompanied by bouts of irritability-small irritations that escalated into angry outbursts toward customers and colleagues. To cope, Arjun began working excessively, arriving early, staying late, and refusing to take breaks. He avoided any opportunity for intimacy with his ex-wife and with friends, fearing that closeness would make him vulnerable. When thoughts of the bomb returned, he would push them aside, telling himself that they were unimportant and would distract him from the present. The belief that he could no longer rely on himself became the lens through which Arjun viewed his world. He started to think that his capacity to keep the bank's finances in order, to serve customers with dignity, and to manage his own life had been irrevocably damaged by the event. "I used to be the one people counted on to keep everything running smoothly," he told himself. "Now I'm just a shadow of my former self." This sense of lost competence and inability to self-reliance intensified his perception that he was under constant threat. The constant checking, the nightly vigilance, and the angry flashes of irritability fed a heightened sense of danger that seemed to permeate every corner of his existence. His belief that he could not depend on his own judgment forced him to remain on high alert, as if any slight deviation could trigger another catastrophe. The relentless sense of threat, in turn, reinforced his negative self-appraisals. Every time he woke to check whether a sound was a vehicle or a threat, he felt his heart sink deeper into the belief that he was unprotected. The more he confirmed that danger lurked around every corner, the stronger his conviction that he was powerless. His belief that he could no longer rely on himself was not merely a thought but a loop that fed into every other symptom. The more he sensed danger, the more he felt incapable, the more he felt incapable, and so on, a tightening cycle that seemed to close around him with each passing day. His maladaptive strategies also reinforced his negative self-appraisals. The overwork he took on, the way he tried to stay ahead of potential threats by being constantly present at the bank, made him feel as though he was failing to meet the standards he had set for himself. He was no longer the efficient teller who calmly handled queues and kept a steady rhythm; he was the one who dreaded being alone with his thoughts, who avoided intimacy to the point of alienation, and who suppressed any memory that might remind him of the terror. These coping mechanisms served as evidence of failure, confirming his belief that he was no longer capable of doing the things that once defined him. The more he worked, the more he missed subtle cues from customers-leading to small errors that he could not excuse. Each error felt like a confirmation that he had let down his own sense of competence and violated the values he once held dear. The consequences of this self-reinforcing cycle seeped into his daily life at the bank. Colleagues noticed his short temper and his tendency to ignore the friendly banter that had once filled the break room. He began arriving later, claiming exhaustion, and then excused himself from meetings or refused to participate in team projects. The subtle but consistent decline in his performance began to haunt him, adding to the feeling that he could no longer rely on himself. His divorce from his wife, a relationship he had once cherished, became a byproduct of his avoidance of intimacy; the fear that closeness would expose his vulnerability left them drifting apart. Today, after months of sleepless nights, constant checking, and an exhausting routine that left him drained, Arjun has finally decided to seek help. The fear that his job will deteriorate further, that he will lose his reputation, and that his sense of safety will vanish entirely keeps him from taking a single step forward. Yet, in the quiet moments of the night, when the house is silent and his thoughts seem to roar louder than the world outside, he longs to feel grounded, to trust his own judgment, and to reclaim a sense of self-worth that the terror had ripped away.
